drills.q: Why chunk documents at all instead of embedding whole documents?
drills.a: Embedding models compress a fixed-size input into a fixed-size vector; a whole long document averaged into one vector loses specific detail, so localized queries score poorly against it. Chunking keeps vectors focused enough for similarity search to localize the right passage.

drills.q: What does overlap between chunks cost you, in storage terms?
drills.a: Storage/embedding compute scales with chunk_size / (chunk_size - overlap); 20% overlap means roughly 25% more chunks than no overlap for the same document.

drills.q: Explain contextual retrieval and why it's affordable at scale.
drills.a: Prepend a short LLM-generated context sentence to each chunk before embedding/BM25 indexing, restoring the anchor lost when a chunk is decontextualized. Affordable because prompt caching lets the whole document be cached once and referenced, not re-sent, per chunk -- about $1.02/million document tokens.

drills.q: How does late chunking differ mechanically from contextual retrieval, and what does it require?
drills.a: Late chunking embeds the whole document first with a long-context model, then mean-pools token embeddings per chunk span -- no LLM call. It requires an embedding model with a long enough context window to see the whole document (e.g. ~8k tokens), unlike contextual retrieval which works with any embedding model but needs an LLM call per chunk.

drills.q: A recall@20 eval looks great but production users complain retrieval misses obvious answers. What's the likely cause and fix?
drills.a: Likely a distribution mismatch -- the eval set was built from documents shorter or differently structured than production documents, so a fixed chunk_size tuned to the eval didn't generalize. Rebuild the eval from real production documents/queries; prefer structural (heading/section) chunking over a fixed length.

drills.q: How does chunk size interact with reranker cost?
drills.a: Rerankers score every candidate chunk, so cost/latency scale roughly linearly with the number of chunks reranked, not their size. Smaller chunk sizes mean more chunks per document at a given retrieval depth, directly increasing reranker load.

drills.q: Design a chunking strategy for legal contracts with embedded financial tables and heavy cross-references ("as defined in Section 4.2").
drills.a: Parse with a layout-aware tool (Unstructured/LlamaParse) so tables extract as structured Markdown. Chunk by section/clause boundary, not fixed length. Apply contextual retrieval to resolve cross-references (this is exactly the decontextualization failure it fixes). Keep small tables whole with repeated headers if spanning chunks. Validate against a recall@k eval built from real contract questions; expect ~800-1000 token chunks given legal prose density.

drills.q: A candidate claims "I always use the smallest possible chunk size for maximum precision." What's wrong with this?
drills.a: Below a certain size, chunks lose surrounding context needed to be independently interpretable (decontextualization), multiply index storage and reranker load, and increase near-duplicate competition for top-k slots from overlapping tiny chunks. There is no universal "maximum precision" size -- it's a corpus-dependent tradeoff surface requiring an eval-driven process.
